stem: A tissue value is outside a published range. Why should it not automatically trigger a recipe change?
choices: Treat the result as unreliable because tissue testing cannot distinguish nutritional status from root-zone effects in a controlled crop.
Interpret the value in the context of sampled tissue position, crop stage, symptom pattern, root-zone conditions, environment, and the reference population before changing the recipe.
Apply the published range directly if the laboratory method is valid, because sampling context mainly affects visual diagnosis rather than tissue concentration.
Assume the out-of-range result reflects meter or laboratory error unless the same element is also abnormal in root-zone solution.
rationale: A tissue result is evidence, but its meaning depends on how the sample was collected and on the biological and production context. Tissue position, stage, cultivar, symptom distribution, root-zone conditions, and environmental factors can all affect concentration and causality. A published range can inform interpretation without proving that changing the recipe will correct the problem. The strongest response integrates the laboratory value with the rest of the diagnostic evidence.
